content: Preterm infants are at risk of developing nutrient deficits, which can lead to growth restriction outside the womb. Providing preterm infants with nutrient-enriched formula, as opposed to standard formula, may enhance nutrient accumulation, promote faster growth rates, and potentially improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of feeding preterm infants with nutrient-enriched formula compared to standard formula on their growth and developmental outcomes. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal standard search strategy. This included searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, as well as reviews of conference proceedings, prior studies, and clinical trial registries. The search covered studies up to November 2018. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of nutrient-enriched formula (containing additional protein, energy, minerals, vitamins, or other nutrients) with standard formula in preterm infants. Data were extracted using Cochrane Neonatal standard methods, and two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and synthesized the data. Risk ratios (RRs), risk differences, and mean differences (MDs) were calculated. The certainty of the evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE methodology. Seven trials involving a total of 590 preterm infants were identified. Most of the infants included in these studies were clinically stable preterm infants with a birth weight of less than 1850 grams. Few participants were extremely preterm, had extremely low birth weight, or were growth-restricted at birth. The trials were conducted over 30 years ago, were funded by the formula industry, and were small in scale with methodological limitations, such as lack of blinding, which could introduce bias into the results. Meta-analyses of in-hospital growth parameters were limited by statistical heterogeneity. There was no evidence to suggest that nutrient-enriched formula affected the time it took for infants to regain their birth weight (MD -1.48 days, 95% CI -4.73 to 1.77). However, low-certainty evidence indicated that nutrient-enriched formula increased in-hospital weight gain rates (MD 2.43 g/kg/day, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.26) and head circumference growth (MD 1.04 mm/week, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.89). There was no significant effect on the average rate of length gain (MD 0.22 mm/week, 95% CI -0.70 to 1.13). Data on growth and developmental outcomes beyond infancy were sparse and did not show consistent effects of nutrient-enriched formula feeding. Two trials provided data on neurodevelopmental outcomes, specifically the Bayley Mental Development Index scores at 18 months post-term, and found no significant effect (MD 2.87, 95% CI -1.38 to 7.12; moderate-certainty evidence). However, infants who received nutrient-enriched formula had higher Bayley Psychomotor Development Index scores at 18 months post-term (MD 6.56, 95% CI 2.87 to 10.26; low-certainty evidence). There was no evidence to suggest an effect on the risk of cerebral palsy (typical RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.07; 2 studies, 377 infants). The available data did not indicate any other significant benefits or harms associated with nutrient-enriched formula feeding. Low-certainty evidence suggested that nutrient-enriched formula might have a modest effect on reducing the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants (typical RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.25; 3 studies, 489 infants). In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that feeding preterm infants with nutrient-enriched formula, compared to standard formula, has only modest effects on growth rates during their initial hospital stay. There is no evidence to support significant effects on long-term growth or developmental outcomes. The certainty of the evidence is low, and these findings should be interpreted with caution. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to address the uncertainties and provide more definitive conclusions.
